profile.reading:
This building at 113 North Oxford Street in Oxford, Wisconsin is the headquarters and central office of Marquette-Adams Telephone Cooperative, a member-owned rural telecommunications cooperative that has operated in the area since 1951, part of the wave of rural telephone cooperatives formed across the upper Midwest in the mid-20th century to bring service to communities that investor-owned phone companies found unprofitable to serve. The cooperative's own materials describe both an older and a newer headquarters building at this Oxford location, indicating the facility has been rebuilt or expanded at least once since the co-op's founding, though a specific construction date for the current building is not published. Like most small rural telephone cooperatives, Marquette-Adams does not operate a dedicated, purpose-built data center in the commercial colocation sense; instead, this headquarters building doubles as the co-op's central office, housing the switching, routing, and network-management equipment that supports its member territory across Marquette County and neighboring areas. In recent years the cooperative has extended service through fiber-to-the-home buildouts, marketed under a "Westfield Project" and similar area-expansion phases, reflecting the broader shift among small rural telecom cooperatives from legacy copper telephone plant to fiber-optic internet, television, and voice service. The cooperative is registered with the Wisconsin Public Service Commission as a certificated telecommunications provider, which is the primary form of public regulatory record available for an operation of this size; unlike investor-owned utilities or large data-center operators, small member-owned cooperatives are not required to and do not publish facility-level specifications such as building square footage, backup power capacity, or cooling design, because the building's core function is as a telephone-company central office rather than as leased or marketed data-center space. What the public record establishes, in short, is an address, a multi-decade operating history rooted in the rural cooperative telephone movement, evidence of at least one facility rebuild, and a present-day service focus on fiber expansion -- but no technical specification sheet exists for this building because none is customarily produced or required for a cooperative central office of this kind.

That gap in published detail is not unusual for the sector: rural telephone cooperatives are member-owned, not investor-owned, and answer to their subscriber-members and state regulators rather than to a market of prospective tenants, so they have neither the incentive nor the obligation that a commercial data-center landlord has to publish a marketing-oriented specification sheet for a building that exists to serve the cooperative's own network rather than to attract outside customers.

reading.body:
Marquette-Adams Telephone Cooperative operates a data-center facility in Wisconsin with zero reported megawatts of capacity, indicating either unreported power draw or a facility too small for public disclosure thresholds.

The cooperative runs its facility from its headquarters in Oxford as a combined central office and data operation, a structure typical of rural telephone utilities that have repurposed legacy telecom infrastructure. Rural cooperatives often lack the capital and grid access to build dedicated, large-scale data centers, so they repurpose existing buildings and connections to serve local enterprise or cloud edge computing needs.

The zero-megawatt rating reflects a gap in how small facilities are tracked. Rural data infrastructure that serves real computing workloads may consume meaningful power but falls below the reporting requirements that apply to larger operators. This obscures the distributed nature of the actual data infrastructure footprint in the United States.

The data does not reveal what workloads this facility serves, what its actual power consumption is, or whether it connects to broader AI compute chains. It confirms only that a rural cooperative has categorized itself as a data-center operator, which is relevant to understanding where compute lives outside major metropolitan clusters.
